Then the picture cracked. A long grey hand with too many fingers reached through it. More hands crept out and turned over her memories like pages.
"So this is what it is," said a voice. It was everywhere. It was not cruel. It sounded very tired. "How curious."
It had no face. It was a vast vortex the colour of twilight, with a thousand dim stars in its heart.
"I am the Will of the Planet."
Vexana had always known. "It was you," she said. "You killed my father."
"I did not know him," said the Will. "I know only the web. He was a thread in it, and it was cut. I do not ask you to forgive me. I only wish you to know that it was not done in malice."
Her hatred drained away. She had expected a monster. She had not expected sorrow. "Why?" she whispered.
It showed her a web of silver light, with a world at every knot.
had grown too heavy, and the web was tilting. "One heavy knot drags the rest," said the Will. "So I cut it down. It is the only way I have found."

"I have chosen you," said the Will. "I heard a clear gold note ring on a rooftop, one summer afternoon. At the other end of it, I found you. You are the dark note that holds the bright one up. You alone can hear me."
"I am nothing like you. I would never cut a thread."
"You have not been asked," said the Will. "Look."
It showed her the street by the lake, burning, and the
"Destruction, as all returns to chaos," said the Will. "This is no judgement. Merely the universe's predetermined execution."
It showed her the roof of the east wing, grey with ash.
lay there in a ring. At the end of the ring lay Guinevere, as if asleep.
Vexana knelt beside her. In her fist, the golden Emblem was dark and cold. A crack ran across it, and the star crumbled to dust.
"You shall witness life's destruction," said the Will, "as all returns to chaos."
"Is this the only way?" she whispered.
"It cannot be stopped. It can only be accompanied."
The Will leaned over her like a tree over a sleeping child. "But when a world falls, I may spare a few

, to rebuild. I can choose them. I could spare Guinevere, if I were given a reason. I have many hands but no mouth. Be my voice." It paused. "A friend. When the time comes, you will say one word, and the one you love will live. Will you accept?"
She almost laughed. The Will meant every word.
Vexana looked at the dust on her palm.

She kept her mind as still as a stone in a pool. Then she lifted her eyes, slowly. Far away, at the heart of the dark, she saw it. It was no bigger than a fist, white and violet and clear as glass. It hung in a ring of pale threads and pulsed, slow and cold.
She did not reach for it. She looked away at once. But she felt the Will's huge attention turn toward her.
"Nothing. I was thinking. I think I would like to say yes."
"Because I love her. You have been through every room in my head. You know it is true."
"I know," said the Will slowly, "that it is true."
It searched her again, gently, like a feather. It found love and grief and fear, and all of it was true. It did not find her plan. She had hidden it in the middle of her love for Guinevere.

"Very well," said the Will. "I am content." It began to sing, and Vexana felt herself come apart and be made again.
She opened her eyes in the void, warm and rested. In the dark, she saw her reflection and did not know it.

The girl was tall, in a black halter bodice that left her shoulders bare. She wore purple gauntlets and a long, see-through purple cape. Her hair was silver-white at the front with one violet streak, then blue-lavender, then magenta at the tips. Small dark horns, edged with gold, swept back from her temples. Her eyes were pink and glowing, calm and sad.
It's only that I've been dressed.

"No. You're not what I thought. I thought you would be terrible."
"I am," said Obsidia. "It is only that I am also tired." Then her smile faded. "You are lying to him."

"It is quite all right. I shall not tell. A liar who knows she is seen is more useful than one who does not." She looked at her own hand, as if it were a stranger's. "There is also a girl on a small green world. She does not do as I tell her. And I have not minded."

"She is a great trial. She is also, I think, the best thing that I have ever made." Obsidia paused. "Remember two things. The Will is always listening, to your thoughts. Learn to think a little to the side of what you mean. And you will be asked to hurt the one you love. You will have no choice. I would like you to remember, when it comes, that it can be survived."
"Because I have done it," said Obsidia.

"It is not my place, miss," he said. "But when you came here, you were angry and proud, and you hit things. Then you found somebody. Since then you have been the happiest, noisiest creature I ever served. That does not go away."
"I let go," said Guinevere. "My fingers slipped."

"You held on. The young lady with the rabbit told me. You held on until she tore herself away. She chose it." He drew a breath. "I once looked for my sister for years. I did not find her. But in the looking, I became a man who does not give up. I think you are the same."
Something in Guinevere's chest broke, like ice on a lake. She wept like a small child. The huge old man knelt on the floor and held her.
"I know," said Harlan. "It is a very good thing, miss, to hold on."
Afterwards, she ate all six biscuits. "I shall bring more at six," said Harlan. "It is not my place."
"It is," said Guinevere. Her voice was hoarse, but it was her own.

at Angela's shoulder. One night, Guinevere sat by the fire, staring at the dark. She had not slept for days. Layla sat down beside her with her arms folded.
"I'm sorry about Vexana," Layla muttered, with her ears bright red. "I've been thinking what I'd do if it were Fanny. I'd be a wreck. I'd be exactly like you."
"It's a confession. You're not allowed to quit. You will eat and sleep. And when you find her, I will beat the pair of you, at once, with one hand."
A small hand crept out and gripped her glove. "Thank you," said Guinevere.
"It's not a favour. It's tactical," said Layla. But she did not pull her hand away.
On the fifth day, they found the gate on a plain of ice. It was a perfect black disc inside a ring of black stones. It reflected nothing.
"It's closed," said Chang'e. "It has been closed since the day of the Breach. It's only a scar." The needle on her instrument lay at zero.
Guinevere held her Emblem out over the black. Nothing changed. "It's not coming from here."
"Up," said Angela. She stood apart, with her head tilted and her eyes half shut. "It's from the sky. North, and very far. It's the same note as the star. It's an answer."

In the attic, the little white doll still swung in the window. She did not cry. She had cried on the ice, with a small stiff hand in hers. She turned her collar to the last of the sun. The Emblem glowed, brighter than before.
And very far above, in the dark, a pair of pink eyes opened. They saw a thin bright thread of light, rising from a tower on a distant shore.
She smiled where no one could see, and went back to her work.

In her second week, Vexana found a secret garden at the top of the Citadel's highest tower. It was open to the stormy sky. One small, crooked, grey-green tree grew in it. It leaned to one side, as if toward a light that was not there. Obsidia sat alone on a bench beside it.
"Why do you keep it?" said Vexana.

"I did not mean it to grow," said Obsidia. "It came up by itself. It leans toward the east, where there has never been a sunrise. It is the most foolish thing I have ever seen. I cannot bear to cut it down."

"I used to hide in a broom cupboard at school," she said. "Then somebody found me. She left me a doughnut."
Obsidia put a hand over her mouth. Her shoulders shook. "A doughnut. It is a very effective weapon."
So Vexana told her about the roller-coaster, the fireworks and the gold star. She did not tell her about the

"I should like to meet her," said Obsidia. "It is the first time in centuries that I have wished to meet a human."
Lightning lit the sky. In its flash, Vexana saw that the leaves of the tree were green.

"Vexana! It's lit! I know you're there!"
But the roof was empty. Far away, on the floor of a black hall, Vexana lay curled up with the giant's head on her shoulder, and sobbed.
A month later, in the garden, Obsidia taught her a board game.

"These are pawns," she said. "They go forward, and they are taken. It is what they are for. But there is one rule. If a pawn crosses the whole board without being taken, it becomes a queen. It is the only rule I like."

"Yes. I do not know whether I want her to cross. She will be very angry with me. She may have to be asked to come home. When she refuses, I shall be obliged to do something about it. I have mapped every answer. I dislike all of them."
"I do not always get what I wish. It is one of the more annoying parts of being a god." She looked at the board. "I should like to have somebody to play with."
Vexana set a rook down in the wrong place. Obsidia laughed, a warm, rueful sound. They played until the storm broke.
She went to the black market in June. The Will had ordered it.

"I'd like to buy something," said Vexana.
"Well," said Selena. "Look who's come to market. Sit down. I don't want money. It's so dull." She smiled. "You look like somebody's schoolgirl."

Vexana's eyes filled with tears. "Oh, I'm sorry," said Selena. "I'm a beast. I'm an Ender, made in a vat. I've a mother, of a kind, who is very old and tired. I'm trying not to be what she wants me to be."
"I know," said Vexana. She threw back her hood.
Selena saw a thin girl with silver hair, small dark horns and pink eyes. She saw exhaustion. She knew it from the inside.
"You've a plan," she said gently. "It shines on you like a bad lie. You're another pawn, like me."
She took a small black box from under the table. In it, on black velvet, lay a thin needle of dark crystal, as long as a hand. "It's a sliver of a

's heart," she said. "It's the part that held the relay. It's the only bit of Ender in the world that's tuned to the Core. It would go to the Core like a needle to a magnet. It's the one thing that could break it."
The needle began to sing, and the orb on Vexana's staff answered.

"I hear the Core in my sleep. It's like a hand on the back of my neck. I'd like it to stop." She pushed the box across the cloth. "It's not for sale. It's a loan. But I want a story in return. When it's all over, tell me how it ended. I'd like to know there's a way out."
is cold and clever," said Selena, "and she plays chess with a pawn. She made me. I'm awfully fond of her. It's the most inconvenient thing."
"She laughed when I put the rook in the wrong place," said Vexana.
"She doesn't laugh!" Selena grinned. "Don't let her see you're fond of her. She'll be insufferable."
They both began to laugh, half sob and half giggle.
Vexana left before dawn, with the box inside her cloak. Selena raised one hand from the table.
Outside, rain fell on the roofs. Far off, a white tower stood against the grey morning. Its green lamp looked like a candle in a window.
Now I only have to get to the heart.
She did not know how. She had a needle in her cloak and a star at her throat. And every night, a voice reached her from very far away.
She laid her hand on the damp wall. "I know," she said aloud, to the tower.

There was no answer. But in the attic, a small gold star flared at the collar of a girl asleep on a camp bed. It had been dim for a hundred nights. Now it burned strong and silver-gold. The girl, with a bear in her arms and dried tears on her cheek, smiled in her sleep.
